strengths: Soundness: The WRITE/READ formulation is coherent and enforces context removal during answering. The strongest comparison controls both the backbone and memory size: in Table 1, GradMem with five updates achieves 99.1% retrieval accuracy on 64 pairs versus 19.3% for one-pass RMT, using the same eight memory vectors. Reporting three-run variability strengthens this result.

Originality: Meta-training an input-level memory initialization and backbone for few-step reconstruction-based writing is a useful synthesis of embedding optimization and meta-learning. The contribution is the demonstrated effectiveness of this few-step regime, rather than gradient-based memory in general.

Significance: The synthetic experiments provide meaningful evidence that the writing mechanism can substantially affect usable memory capacity. Figure 4 also demonstrates that some trained models benefit from additional inference-time optimization without updating backbone weights.

Presentation and limitations: The equations and diagrams make the method understandable. The paper candidly discusses higher-order differentiation costs and supplies attention implementation benchmarks and cached-context latency comparisons. These are useful engineering contributions. The benchmark-based research raises no apparent material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness and presentation: Several natural-language claims contradict Table 2. Section 3.5 says one-step GradMem outperforms RMT on Short SQuAD, but its EM is 38.1 versus 42.6. Increasing K does not improve the reported bAbI results: QA2 decreases from 94.2 to 93.9 and QA3 from 80.0 to 79.3, with the other tasks unchanged. GradMem also trails RMT on QA3 and slightly on language modeling. The increased-K SQuAD result of 54.9 is encouraging, but the evidence supports mixed downstream benefits rather than generally favorable scaling.

Reproducibility: Appendix B omits important training specifications, including outer-loop optimizer settings, training duration, batch sizes, dataset sizes and split protocols, and the exact K values behind Table 2's 'increased K' row. It is unclear whether that row changes training K, evaluation K, or both. The manuscript states that supplementary code is supplied, but that code was not available in the provided material, so these details could not be verified.

Soundness: The claim that gradient writing is 'more expressive' than forward computation exceeds the experiment. Matching memory size is valuable, but a gradient update costs more than a forward update, and repeated RMT writes do not exhaust possible forward encoders. A compute-matched comparison with a stronger encoder or established learned context compressor would better separate the benefit of the proposed writing rule from additional computation and training choices.

Significance: Natural-language evaluation is limited to small models and short contexts. Short SQuAD uses the answer-containing sentence, averaging approximately 40 tokens, with 32 memory tokens; language modeling compresses only 128 context tokens. These experiments establish applicability but do not establish usefulness for the long-document and reusable-context applications motivating the paper. No evaluation demonstrates one learned memory answering a diverse set of questions about a long document.

Soundness: Inference-time scaling is conditional. Figure 4 shows that the 64-pair model trained with K=1 declines from 58.6% to 53.1% when evaluated with five steps. The 'best of' evaluation ranges do not specify an independent selection procedure or deployable stopping rule. Claims of reliable improvement should distinguish fixed-step results from retrospectively selected maxima.

Reproducibility and efficiency: The 'without meta-learning' ablation is described both as a first-order approximation and as disabling the meta-learning path, without specifying which gradients remain. These alternatives have different interpretations. Separately, the latency experiment uses K=1, whereas the strongest retrieval results require K=5; it therefore does not establish the compute–accuracy trade-off of the best-performing configuration. Persistent memory size should also be distinguished explicitly from the per-layer prefix cache used for efficient READ operations.

strengths: Soundness: The WRITE/READ formulation is coherent, with an explicit reconstruction objective and differentiation through memory updates. Table 1 provides substantial evidence for improved synthetic retrieval at matched architecture and memory size: with 64 pairs, five-step GradMem achieves 99.1±0.3% versus 19.3±3.1% for one-pass RMT. Reporting three-run variability is helpful.

Originality: Combining input-level memory optimization with meta-training for effective few-step writing is a useful contribution. The distinction from per-layer test-time training and expensive embedding reconstruction is explained, and Figure 4 demonstrates that some trained models benefit from additional inference-time updates.
Presentation: The central equations and diagrams clearly distinguish shared model parameters from per-context memory. The context-removal protocol makes the information bottleneck explicit.

Limitations and ethics: The paper candidly discusses higher-order training costs and supplies attention implementation benchmarks and cached-context latency comparisons. These are constructive disclosures. The described benchmark experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness and presentation: Section 3.5 contradicts Table 2 on important findings. It states that one-step GradMem outperforms RMT on Short SQuAD, whereas the scores are 38.1% versus 42.6%. It also claims improvement with larger K on bAbI, but QA2 decreases from 94.2% to 93.9%, QA3 decreases from 80.0% to 79.3%, and the other tasks are unchanged. These discrepancies materially overstate the evidence for language-task gains.

Soundness: The broad claim that gradient writing is more expressive than forward-only computation is not established by the comparisons. Matching memory size and update count does not match computation: gradient updates include backward passes, and meta-training adds substantial cost. Repeated RMT writes are useful controls, but their unstable results and incomplete coverage do not establish a general limitation of forward writers. Accuracy–compute comparisons with adequately tuned baselines are needed.

Reproducibility: Table 2 never specifies the K used for its 'increased K' results or clearly distinguishes training-time from evaluation-time increases. Appendix B omits essential outer-loop optimization settings, training budgets, dataset sizes/splits, and precise implementation details for the 'w/o meta-learning' ablation. Source code is stated to be supplementary, but it was not available in the supplied material; the manuscript alone does not adequately specify these experiments.

Soundness: Figure 4 reports 'best of 0..10/20/30' results without explaining how the step count is selected or whether selection uses held-out validation data. This leaves the deployable compute–accuracy tradeoff unclear. Additional updates also fail to improve the 64-pair model trained with K=1, so improvement is conditional rather than consistently established.

Significance: The natural-language evaluation demonstrates limited practical advantage. Short SQuAD supplies the answer-containing sentence and uses approximately 40 context tokens with 32 memory tokens. On the longer bAbI QA3 task, GradMem substantially trails RMT and ARMT; on language modeling it does not improve over either. These experiments support a narrow proof of concept, but do not yet establish useful compression of realistic long documents or reusable memories across diverse queries.

Originality and evaluation: The paper acknowledges closely related embedding optimization, autoencoding compression, and test-time learning methods, but provides no direct comparison with these closest alternatives. This leaves the benefit attributable specifically to the proposed few-step meta-training approach insufficiently isolated.

Efficiency: Appendix D usefully measures cached-context baselines, but its latency experiment uses K=1, whereas the strongest retrieval results require K=5 or more. It does not jointly report task accuracy, total latency, and actual serving memory for the successful configurations. Consequently, the measured speedups do not establish the practical efficiency of the configurations supporting the main accuracy claims.

strengths: Soundness: The core method is clearly formulated: optimize prefix memory using context reconstruction, then train through those updates using downstream supervision. The context-removal evaluation directly tests whether useful information passes through the memory.

Empirical contribution: Table 1 shows substantial gains over RMT with the same backbone and eight memory vectors. At 32 key–value pairs, one-step GradMem achieves 86.9% accuracy versus 44.3% for RMT; five-step GradMem reaches 99.1% at 64 pairs. Reporting three-run variability strengthens these results.

Originality and significance: Combining model-level reconstruction, input-level memory, and few-step meta-learning is a useful contribution relative to the cited iterative embedding-compression and layer-level TTT approaches. The synthetic experiments provide evidence that the write mechanism materially affects usable memory capacity.

Presentation and limitations: The WRITE/READ decomposition and equations are accessible. The paper explicitly acknowledges higher-order training costs and includes attention-kernel benchmarks and cached-context latency comparisons in Appendices C–D. These are useful supporting analyses. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness of the broader comparison: Matching memory size and update count does not match computation, because a gradient write includes backward computation. The repeated-RMT results are also unstable, including 60.0±42.0 at 16 pairs. Without comparisons at matched compute budgets and clearer baseline tuning details, the experiments establish superiority over the evaluated RMT configurations, not the broader claim that gradient writing is inherently more expressive than forward-only computation.

Natural-language claims exceed the evidence. Section 3.5 says one-step GradMem outperforms RMT on Short SQuAD, but Table 2 reports 38.1% versus 42.6%. Increasing K improves Short SQuAD substantially, but does not improve bAbI QA2 or QA3; QA3 remains substantially below RMT and ARMT. Language-modeling cross-entropy is also slightly worse than RMT. These results support selective usefulness rather than consistent downstream gains.

Significance at realistic compression scales remains uncertain. Short SQuAD supplies the answer-containing sentence, averaging approximately 40 tokens, with 32 memory tokens. The language-modeling experiment compresses only 128 context tokens. These are legitimate controlled settings, but they do not establish the long-context, reusable-document benefits motivating the paper. The latency experiments are not paired with accuracy measurements at the corresponding longer context lengths.

Test-time scaling needs a clearer evaluation protocol. Figure 4 reports 'best of 0..10/20/30' without explaining how the iteration is selected or whether selection uses held-out validation data. This matters for deployability because downstream answers are unavailable during writing. Scaling is also not uniformly beneficial: the 64-pair model trained with K=1 falls from 58.6% at one evaluation step to 53.1% at five.

Reproducibility is insufficiently specified in the manuscript. Appendix B gives useful architectural choices and an inner-learning-rate range, but omits important optimizer, training-budget, dataset-size, and selection details. Table 2 does not specify the values or training/evaluation roles of 'increased K.' Supplementary code is stated to be provided, but these essential experimental settings should also be explicit in the paper.

The meta-learning ablation is ambiguous: Table 1 calls it 'w/o meta-learning,' Section 3.3 describes a first-order approximation, and Appendix B describes disabling the meta-learning path. These are not necessarily equivalent procedures. Consequently, the evidence does not cleanly establish whether the observed failure comes from removing second-order terms, removing adaptation-dependent learning altogether, or another implementation choice.

strengths: Soundness: The WRITE/READ formulation is coherent, with context-only reconstruction updates and downstream prediction after context removal. The principal matched-memory result is substantial: at 32 key–value pairs, GradMem achieves 86.9% accuracy with one update and 99.9% with five, versus 44.3% for RMT using the same eight memory vectors (Table 1). Results include variability across three runs.

Originality: The useful contribution is the combination of input-level memory optimization, a model-level reconstruction objective, and second-order meta-training for few-step writing. This is a meaningful development beyond simply optimizing embeddings for reconstruction. The first-order ablation and input-level versus per-layer comparison help explain the design.

Significance: The experiments establish a promising mechanism for improving retrieval under a fixed persistent-memory budget. The Short SQuAD improvement over RMT, 54.9% versus 42.6%, also provides evidence that the benefit is not confined to synthetic retrieval.

Presentation and limitations: The method, equations, and algorithm are generally clear. The appendices provide useful memory-size sweeps, TTT/LaCT comparisons, and measured latency analyses. The authors appropriately acknowledge second-order training costs and task-dependent gains. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is insufficient for the central empirical comparison. Appendix B specifies architectures and some inner-loop hyperparameters but omits outer-loop optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, training budgets, batch sizes, and precise curriculum transitions. Dataset sizes/splits and checkpoint-selection procedures are also inadequately specified. The manuscript's repeated 'Code is available at' statements contain no usable link. These omissions matter particularly because training stability, initialization, and curriculum affect the reported results.

Soundness of the comparative claim: Matching memory and architecture supports a memory-efficiency advantage over the tested RMT implementation, but does not establish that gradient writing is generally 'more expressive' than forward computation. A gradient update includes backward computation, so equal update counts are not compute matched. Repeated RMT writes are a useful control, but no accuracy comparison matches total WRITE compute or documents comparable tuning/training budgets. The conclusion should be narrowed or supported by stronger controls.

Inference-time scaling is less reliable than the headline suggests. Figure 4 includes 'best of 0..10/20/30' accuracies without specifying an independent selection procedure or a deployable stopping rule. It also shows that extra steps hurt the 64-pair model trained with K=1. Fixed-step gains in other settings are convincing, but oracle-style maxima and correlations with reconstruction loss do not establish a generally reliable inference-time improvement policy.

Practical significance remains preliminary. Short SQuAD uses the answer-containing sentence, averaging roughly 40 tokens, with 32 memory tokens; this is a limited test of reusable context compression. GradMem underperforms RMT on bAbI QA3 and essentially ties it on language modeling. Appendix I demonstrates larger-model reconstruction only on short spans, whereas the 4k–16k latency benchmarks report no corresponding task quality. Consequently, those timings do not yet demonstrate useful long-context compression at the reported break-even points.

Originality is better supported conceptually than experimentally relative to the closest compression approaches. Related work discusses optimized embeddings, ICAE, and Cartridges, but the evaluation does not directly quantify the advantage over a comparable embedding-optimization or autoencoding baseline. Together with the reproducibility and comparison issues, this leaves revisions necessary before the broader conclusions can be relied upon.

strengths: Soundness: The controlled associative-retrieval results provide substantial evidence for improved memory utilization. With the same architecture and eight memory vectors, GradMem achieves 96.3% accuracy versus RMT’s 45.5% at 16 pairs; five WRITE steps reach 99.1% at 64 pairs (Table 1). Results include variability across three runs.

Originality: Meta-training input-level memory and model parameters so that a few reconstruction-gradient steps produce useful downstream representations is a meaningful synthesis of embedding optimization and meta-learning. Its contribution is the few-step writing mechanism and its empirical behavior, rather than test-time optimization itself.

Significance: The memory-size sweeps, second-order-gradient ablation, input-level versus per-layer comparison, and additional TTT baselines provide useful evidence about compact memory design. The Short SQuAD improvement over RMT, 54.9% versus 42.6%, also demonstrates utility beyond synthetic retrieval.

Presentation and limitations: The WRITE/READ formulation and mathematical description are clear. The paper explicitly acknowledges higher-order training costs and task-dependent gains, and provides attention benchmarks and cached-context latency comparisons. These are constructive limitations analyses. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is materially incomplete. Despite Appendix B’s title, the manuscript omits outer-loop optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, training duration, task-training batch sizes, dataset sizes/splits, and detailed curriculum schedules. The repeated 'Code is available at' statements contain no usable link. Minimal pseudocode does not resolve these omissions, particularly given the reported training instability and sensitivity of competing methods.

The evidence supports superiority over the evaluated forward writers at fixed stored-state size, but not the broader claim that gradient writing is inherently 'more expressive than a fixed forward computation' (Sections 2.2 and 3.3). WRITE steps are not compute-matched: each GradMem step includes backpropagation through the model. Training budgets and baseline tuning are insufficiently documented, and repeated RMT writes do not exhaust possible iterative forward encoders. An accuracy-versus-compute comparison would better isolate the claimed advantage.

Practical long-context significance remains unestablished. Short SQuAD uses the gold answer-containing sentence, averaging about 40 tokens, with 32 memory tokens. This is a useful controlled task but provides limited evidence for compressing realistic documents. On the longest bAbI task, GradMem scores about 79–80%, below RMT’s 87.9%; language-modeling performance essentially matches RMT. Appendix I extends model scale but evaluates reconstruction of only 8–64 tokens. The longer-context latency experiments do not establish corresponding answer quality.

Inference-step scaling needs a clearer evaluation protocol. Figure 4 reports 'best of 0..10/20/30' without specifying whether step selection uses validation data, reconstruction loss, or evaluation accuracy. The distinction matters for deployable gains. Improvements are also not universal: the 64-pair model trained with one step worsens when evaluated with two to five steps. The paper acknowledges some heterogeneity, but several captions and conclusions state the scaling benefit too broadly.

The empirical relationship to closely related context-compression methods remains incomplete. Appendix A discusses ICAE, SelfCP, and prior reconstruction-based embedding optimization, but does not compare against them. Such comparisons would help establish whether meta-trained gradient writing improves the quality–memory–compute trade-off beyond the selected recurrent baselines. Together with the missing training recipe, this leaves revisions necessary before others can reliably build on an otherwise promising contribution.

strengths: Originality: The combination of a single input-level memory, context-reconstruction updates, and second-order meta-training is a useful contribution beyond prior embedding optimization and layer-local test-time training. Targeting effective writing in only 1–5 steps is particularly compelling.

Soundness: The strongest evidence is the controlled, matched-memory retrieval comparison. With eight memory vectors, GradMem achieves 96.3% accuracy on 16 pairs versus RMT’s 45.5%; five updates reach 99.1% on 64 pairs. Three-run reporting and ablations on second-order training, memory size, and memory placement strengthen this result.

Significance: Short SQuAD improves from RMT’s 42.6% to 54.9% with increased WRITE steps. Appendix I also demonstrates short-text reconstruction using frozen 1B–3B READ models, supporting applicability beyond small synthetic models.

Presentation and limitations: The WRITE/READ formulation, equations, and minimal algorithm are clear. The paper explicitly acknowledges training overhead and task-dependent gains, and includes measured latency experiments. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is the decisive weakness. Appendix B specifies architectures and some inner-loop settings but omits outer-loop optimizer settings, training budgets, batch sizes for accuracy experiments, and sufficiently detailed dataset construction and validation procedures. Exact selected retrieval learning rates and curriculum schedules are also missing. The promised code links are blank. These omissions matter especially because the paper reports substantial training instability and curriculum dependence.

The evidence supports superiority over the evaluated writers at fixed stored-memory size, but not the broader claim that gradient writing is intrinsically more expressive than forward computation. A gradient step includes a backward pass, so equal update counts do not match computation. Repeated RMT writes are also unstable and incompletely evaluated. A comparison against better-tuned forward compressors under matched compute, or narrower claims, is needed.

Test-time scaling is less reliable than some claims suggest. In Figure 4, the 64-pair model trained with K=1 worsens when evaluated with additional steps. Columns reporting 'best of 0..10/20/30' lack a stated validation-based selection or deployable stopping rule. Table 1 primarily changes training and evaluation K together, so it cannot independently establish inference-only scaling.

Natural-language evidence remains mixed and narrowly scoped. Short SQuAD supplies the gold-answer-containing sentence and uses 32 memory tokens for approximately 40 context tokens. On bAbI QA3, GradMem achieves roughly 79–80% versus RMT’s 87.9%, while language-modeling performance is essentially tied with RMT. These experiments demonstrate feasibility but do not establish a general advantage for realistic document compression.

The long-context efficiency measurements are not paired with task-quality measurements at the same operating points. Appendix D times contexts up to 16k tokens with eight memory tokens and one update, whereas larger-model accuracy experiments reconstruct only short spans. Thus, the measured latency break-even points do not yet demonstrate useful, quality-preserving long-context inference. Overall, the promising core result warrants further development, but the reporting and evidential gaps need resolution before acceptance.
